title: Chauri Chaura
subtitle: The fire, the halt and the argument over non-violence

context.title: Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh
context.text: The Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre turned constitutional protest into a mass movement and gave Gandhi his moral vocabulary for non-cooperation.

context.title: Non-cooperation launched
context.text: Gandhi launched non-cooperation on 4 September 1920, asking Indians to withdraw cooperation from British courts, schools, councils and goods.

context.title: Violence elsewhere
context.text: The Moplah Rebellion and the Prince of Wales riots showed that mass action could turn violent far from Gandhi's control, months before Chauri Chaura.

context.title: Chauri Chaura, 4 February
context.text: A crowd of peasants burned the Chauri Chaura police station after police fired on them, killing 22 policemen and three civilians.

context.title: The halt and the arrest, 12 February
context.text: Gandhi halted non-cooperation nationally and was arrested the same day; he was sentenced to six years on 18 March for seditious material.

context.title: Trial and gallows
context.text: A trial lasting eight months convicted 170 and acquitted 47; nineteen were hanged between 2 and 11 July 1923.

debates.question: Was Gandhi's decision to stop non-cooperation a defence of non-violence or a retreat that demobilised a winning movement?
debates.hook: The movement was at its widest when a single district burned; the order to stop came within eight days.
debates.stakes: If restraint was courage, it cost the movement its momentum; if it was retreat, it saved the moral claim that later won independence.
debates.uncomfortable: Nehru and most Congress workers in prison called the decision hasty and incorrect, so the disagreement was inside the movement, not only outside it.
debates.whatWouldChange: Evidence that violence was spreading beyond isolated districts, or evidence that a local containment could have kept the national movement intact.
caseFor: Gandhi had already seen the Moplah Rebellion and the Prince of Wales riots pull mass action away from non-violence.
A leader who cannot restrain a crowd loses the moral distinction that made non-cooperation more than a riot.
caseAgainst: The incident was local; a national halt punished hundreds of thousands of disciplined protesters for one district's violence.
The movement was at peak support, and the halt handed the initiative back to the colonial state.

debates.question: Did the Chauri Chaura trial deliver justice, or a colonial warning?
debates.hook: The trial ran eight months, convicted 170 and hanged nineteen, while six of the accused died in police custody.
debates.stakes: A legal process that punishes a crowd collectively sets the template for how the state treats political violence.
debates.uncomfortable: The same authorities built a memorial to the dead policemen in 1923, while the accused waited for appeals.
debates.whatWouldChange: A demonstrable individual trial record that matched each sentence to a specific act, rather than to membership in a crowd.
caseFor: The court acquitted 47 of the accused, which shows that the trial distinguished between participants.
The Allahabad High Court reviewed the death sentences on appeal before the hangings in July 1923.
caseAgainst: Six died in custody before judgment, and 170 were convicted in a process that treated a crowd as a conspiracy.
The 1923 memorial to the policemen was built while the condemned were still being hanged, which made the state's version of the dead the official one.

debates.question: Was the violence at Chauri Chaura a betrayal of non-cooperation, or a product of the movement's own mass politics?
debates.hook: The crowd came to the bazaar to protest an attack on pickets; by afternoon it had burned the police station.
debates.stakes: If mass politics cannot control its own crowd, every mobilisation carries the seed of the incident.
debates.uncomfortable: The police had already killed three protesters before the station was set alight, so the crowd's violence followed the state's violence.
debates.whatWouldChange: A record showing that the crowd was organised by local leaders who planned the arson, rather than a spontaneous reaction to the firing.
caseFor: Non-cooperation asked millions to confront the state; a crowd trained in confrontation can turn when the state fires first.
The immediate trigger was police firing that killed three, so the arson was a retaliation inside the same afternoon.
caseAgainst: Gandhi's method depended on accepting blows without returning them; the crowd's action inverted the method at the first test.
Local leaders had warned that the movement's discipline was thin in Gorakhpur, and the incident proved them right.

debates.question: Who owns the memory of Chauri Chaura: the policemen's memorial or the martyrs' minaret?
debates.hook: The British dedicated a memorial to the dead policemen in 1923; local inhabitants built a 12.2-metre minaret to the hanged in 1973.
debates.stakes: The two memorials do not just remember different people; they disagree about who was defending order and who was sacrificing for freedom.
debates.uncomfortable: The minaret depicts a figure hanging with a noose, which makes the execution itself the monument.
debates.whatWouldChange: A shared memorial that names both the policemen and the protesters, or a local archive that treats the incident as a tragedy rather than a victory.
caseFor: The minaret is a local assertion that the hanged were martyrs, built with Rs 13,500 raised by popular subscription.
The British memorial was dedicated by the colonial authorities, so it records the state's dead, not the town's.
caseAgainst: The policemen were also local men with families; a memorial that ignores them repeats the silence of the trial.
A monument that centres the noose keeps the violence as the town's defining image, rather than the argument about non-violence.
